title: Earth-Moon light time, 2026-2029 (JPL Horizons)

source.publisher: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Solar System Dynamics Group

source.citation: Giorgini, JD and JPL Solar System Dynamics Group, NASA/JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System, <https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/>, data retrieved 2026-Nov-14. Observer table, target Moon (301), center Earth geocenter (500@399), quantities 20, 21, daily. Accessed through the Horizons API (https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api), signature "NASA/JPL Horizons API" version 1.2.

caveats: Ephemeris output, not a measurement: JPL Horizons observer table for the Moon (301) from the Earth geocenter (500@399), one sample per day at 00:00 UTC.
Range is Earth-center to Moon-center; a ground antenna or a lunar-surface crew differs by at most about one Earth radius plus one Moon radius (about 0.03 light-seconds).
Daily samples under-resolve the monthly perigee/apogee cycle only slightly; interpolate linearly between days.
Light time is geometric (range / c); relay geometry (e.g. a lunar far-side relay) is not modelled.
A planetary ephemeris does not go stale on a clock (stale_after is null): the values are valid until coverage.stop.

horizons.units_conversion: Units conversion: 1 au= 149597870.700 km, c= 299792.458 km/s

from: horizons header: Units conversion: 1 au= 149597870.700 km, c= 299792.458 km/s

au_km.basis: as printed in the Horizons header

column_basis.range_km: derived: range_au x au_km, rounded to 1 km
column_basis.one_way_light_time_s: derived: range_au x light_time_per_au_s, rounded to 0.1 ms

light_time_cross_check.resolution_note: Horizons prints light time in minutes with 8 decimals (6e-7 s), so agreement at ~3e-7 s is agreement to its last digit.

data.conjunctions_note: None by construction: the Moon is never behind the Sun as seen from Earth. Sun-in-antenna-beam noise near new Moon is not modelled.
